title: Nice, not needed
hook: Stoics prefer health and wealth but don't stake their happiness on them

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four virtues, wisdom, courage, justice and self-control. Your line was four virtues. Which one did you carry, and where did it show up? Day two hundred eighty-four.

Two days ago the Stoics told us health and money aren't truly good. You might have thought: fine, easy to say from a marble bench. So does that mean a Stoic shrugs at a broken leg? Turns down a raise? Lives on cold water and gravel? No. And the reason is a careful piece of sorting. It's about the difference between something you'd like and something you need. A warm coat on a cold day. A good night's sleep. A full fridge. Nice. Very nice. Today: adiaphora.
screen: `SO A STOIC SHRUGS AT A BROKEN LEG?` → `NO.` → `ADIAPHORA.`

segments.voice: Adiaphora is Greek for indifferents, things that don't make a difference. Not to your comfort; they make a big difference there. They make no difference to whether you're a good person. Health, wealth, reputation, even life itself: all indifferent in that one sense. But the Stoics sorted the indifferents. Some are preferred: health over sickness, enough money over poverty, friends over loneliness. It's natural and sensible to pick those, and a Stoic will. Others are dispreferred, and it's sensible to avoid them. Zeno explained the word preferred with a picture from a royal court, which Cicero passes on. At court, the ministers and nobles are promoted, placed near the throne. But none of them is the king. Health and money are like that: high in rank, never the ruler. Only character sits on the throne. Seneca was a very rich man, and in his essay On the Happy Life he answers critics who threw that at him. His answer is roughly: the wise person may own wealth, but wealth must not own him. Epictetus gives the gentlest picture of all, in his Handbook: behave in life as at a banquet. When a dish comes around to you, reach out and take a polite share. If it passes you by, don't grab at it. If it hasn't reached you yet, don't stretch across the table. Enjoy what's in front of you. Just don't stake your happiness on the next plate. That's the whole teaching in three words. Nice, not needed.
screen: `ADIAPHORA — INDIFFERENTS.` · `PREFERRED, AND DISPREFERRED.` · `NEAR THE THRONE, NEVER THE KING.` · `TAKE A SHARE AT THE BANQUET.` · then, large: `NICE, NOT NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Choose one comfort that's with you right now. The chair under you. A warm drink. The quiet in the room. Let yourself enjoy it fully for a few breaths. Really enjoy it. Then, gently, imagine it gone: the chair harder, the drink cold, the room loud. You'd still be you. Come back to the comfort, and hold it a little more lightly. The bell holds the time.
Adiaphora. Greek for indifferents: things like health and wealth that are worth preferring but don't make you good or bad. Today's word.
Your line: nice, not needed. Enjoy one comfort today, a good meal, a hot shower, a quiet minute, and hold it lightly, like a dish at the banquet. Day two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Stoic practitioners enjoy comforts and pursue sensible goals like health and income, while reminding themselves that these are preferred, not necessary for a good life.

what a scholar hears: Zeno's proēgmena, 'promoted' things, named after courtiers ranked near the king (Cicero, On Ends 3.52).
